newsitem.title: FRANCE: Credit Lyonnais says state will recoup money - paper. [CORRECTED 15:01 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Credit Lyonnais says state will recoup money - paper. [CORRECTED 15:01 GMT]

text.p: Credit Lyonnais head Jean Peyrelevade said on Friday the state-controlled bank will need to be recapitalised to be privatised but the government will get all of the money back -- and more -- when it sells it.
"The revenue from the privatisation will much higher than the recapitalisation" and the impact on public finances "will be positive," Peyrelevade told the afternoon daily Le Monde.

The bank chairman's comments came after Credit Lyonnais announced on Thursday a modest 1996 net attributable profit of 202 million francs, up from 13 million in 1995, and a strong underlying performance.
The bank, poised to receive another state aid package to ready it for sale, forecast net profit would be in the "billions" of francs next year.

After suggesting last year the bank might need a tier one ratio of 5.5 to 6.0 percent to match its rivals' solvency standards and attract a buyer, Peyrelevade said a ratio of slightly more than 4.5 percent could not be sufficient. (Corrects from "could" to "could not").
The bank's tier one ratio now stands at 4.6 percent.
This would imply a need for a state injection of funds. (Corrects from "need for a smaller state injection" to "need for a state injection".)
Last year, the bank estimated it would take 7-8 billion francs to raise the tier one ratio by one percentage point.
The solvency ratio issue, he said, could be settled just before privatisation. With privatisation more than a year away, "no one can predict under what conditions it will be done".

In addition to boosting the bank's solvency ratios, the government will also likely have to inject money to offset the impact from capital losses on asset sales the European Commission is expected to demand in exchange for approving the newest state aid package, the third in four years.
Peyrelevade said he believed the bank should be ready for privatisation in 1998 or 1999.
He said the bank would continue to make disposals "at a rhythm which favours realising the value of those assets considered non-strategic".
He said certain such assets were acquired at the peak of the market and their sale would mean large capital losses.

"We have to reach agreement with the state and with Brussels in the coming months on the way to compensate those capital losses. As long as I do not know exactly how the compensation will be done, there's uncertainty weighing on our 1997 results."

Peyrelevade said the bank had given its recovery plan to the government but the proposal had not yet been forwarded to Brussels. "We're still working on a certain number of problems," he said, alluding to the difficulty over disposals.
The government initially promised the plan to Brussels by the end of March but a source said this week it might not be submitted before early April.
